stories.title: Colombia’s new president Abelardo de la Espriella announces immigration crackdown
stories.summary: Far-right leader echoes ally Donald Trump and says operations to ‘track down illegal immigrants’ should begin this week, amid earthquake aftermath Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, has announced a crackdown on immigrants, ordering authorities to detain and deport people who are in the country irregularly or have committed crimes. In office for just over two weeks, the millionaire former lawyer made the announcement on Sunday as the country continued to grapple with the aftermath of a 7.4-magnitude earthquake on 10 August that killed more than 300 people and destroyed more than 30,000 homes. stories.title: Search continues in Tunisia as migrant boat sinking sparks protests
stories.summary: Tunisia’s Ben Guerdane reels from violent protests after boat carrying 15 people sinks, killing at least 12. Volunteers in Tunisia have continued the search for two people still missing after a boat carrying 15 migrants sank off the country’s southeastern coast, as the city of Ben Guerdane reeled from violent protests sparked by the tragedy. Footage, verified by Al Jazeera, showed volunteers in the city of Zarzis heading out to sea on fishing boats on Monday to search for the missing. The migrant boat, believed to be headed towards Italy, sank late on Friday after setting off from a location between Zarzis and Ben Guerdane with 15 mostly young people on board. It sank about 14 nautical miles (26km) off the coast of Zarzis. Only one person survived, having drifted at sea for about 48 hours before being rescued by a commercial vessel, according to Tunisian media. The bodies of 12 people were recovered by Sunday, the Tunisian National Guard said. The deaths have sparked a wave of grief and anger, triggering violent protests in Ben Guerdane on Sunday night. According to the Tunisian National Guard, some 14 people on the boat were from Ben Guerdane, and one was from Zarzis. The protesters burned tyres and blocked roads, while police responded by firing tear gas to disperse the crowds. The protesters demanded better living conditions and economic development, saying a lack of opportunities and years of marginalisation are pushing young people to undertake dangerous sea crossings to Europe in search of a better life. Mostafa Abdelkebir, the head of the Tunisian Observatory for Human Rights, said those on board included seven members of the same family.

stories.title: How Canada could hit back to hurt the US economy - and Trump
stories.summary: What leverage does Canada, which sells about 70% of its goods to the US, actually have in this spiraling trade dispute with its southern neighbour, who also happens to be the world's largest economy? Canada is the top customer for 26 US states, including Maine, Michigan, and Wisconsin. And it is in the top three for 45 of the 50 American states, suggesting Prime Minister Mark Carney has room to manoeuver in a trade fight. For now, Carney's planned Canadian retaliatory duties are strategic "dollar-for-dollar" countermeasures focused on steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, electronics, pulp and paper - though the list is still being finalised. Polls suggest a majority of Canadians would be unhappy if his government went in the other direction and made significant concessions to the US. That sentiment is shared by Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of Trump's most vocal critics north of the border, who responded to the tariff threats by telling the US president to "kiss my ass". Here are some areas that Canada can apply economic pressure. Carney noted on Saturday that Canada supplies the vast majority of US natural gas and electricity imports and about 60% of crude oil imports. "I don't think they want us to stop sending any of that energy," he said. Squeezing the US on energy is not in the current countermeasures, although various political officials have said explicitly it wasn't ruled out - and not all provincial premiers have been keen to use that leverage. Ford, whose Ontario province is home to Canada's auto manufacturing industry, is open to how far the dispute could go and said that an "energy surcharge is on the table". He briefly floated a 25% surcharge in 2025 on all electricity exports to the United States, which his government estimated would have impacted 1.5 million homes and businesses in Michigan, Minnesota and New York.

stories.title: Snoring, subways and stealth ads: How big pharma targets China's waistline
stories.summary: Weight-loss drugmakers in China use indirect advertising in public places to raise obesity awareness, as direct prescription drug ads are banned. Major firms like Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly, Pfizer, and Innovent compete with once-weekly GLP-1 injections amid rising obesity rates. Companies adapt communication strategies to educate the public while navigating legal limits, sometimes sparking concerns over borderline drug promotion. Weight-loss drugmakers, vying to tighten the belts of Chinese consumers, are promoting obesity awareness in metro stations, exercise studios and soccer stadiums as local restrictions prevent the direct advertising of prescription medicine in the world’s second-largest drug market. China’s rate of overweight or obese people could reach more than 65 per cent by 2030, the country’s National Health Commission has said. Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly, Pfizer and local firm Innovent Biologics are competing for market share with their versions of once-weekly GLP-1 weight-loss injections in China. Lilly led the once-weekly GLP-1 sales on Alibaba’s Tmall e-commerce platform and JD.com in the second quarter, according to Jefferies. China does not allow drug companies to advertise prescription medicine directly to consumers. They can provide information to the public about the risks of specific diseases and recommend that they engage with doctors. Campaigns cannot mention product names, but might indirectly encourage people to seek help. “Don’t forget to pay attention to Dad’s snoring and promptly visit a respiratory department or sleep centre,” a banner with a Lilly logo advised commuters recently at a metro station in Shanghai’s central Jingan district. Snoring is a common symptom of sleep apnea, which is strongly linked to being overweight.
